### Data model & types
```swift
// MARK: - The seam

/// The kid's library, whatever is actually holding it. Callers never ask which
/// provider something lives in; they ask the merged store.
protocol LibraryProvider: Sendable {
    var id: LibraryProviderID { get }
    var capabilities: LibraryCapabilities { get }

    func favorites() async throws -> [FavoriteRow]
    func addFavorite(_ item: CatalogItem) async throws
    func removeFavorite(_ id: CatalogID) async throws

    func playlists() async throws -> [PlaylistRow]
    func createPlaylist(named: String, songs: [CatalogItem]) async throws -> PlaylistRow
    func addToPlaylist(_ handle: PlaylistHandle, song: CatalogItem) async throws
    func removeFromPlaylist(_ handle: PlaylistHandle, song: CatalogID) async throws
    func renamePlaylist(_ handle: PlaylistHandle, to name: String) async throws
    func deletePlaylist(_ handle: PlaylistHandle) async throws
}

enum LibraryProviderID: String, Sendable {
    case cloudKit      // ours; ALWAYS live
    case appleMusic    // live when isSharedDevice == false, which is the default
}

/// What a provider can actually do.
///
/// Absence is not failure — it is a provider sitting one operation out while
/// the others carry it. Two gaps are Apple's and permanent: an artist has no
/// "add to library" form, and MusicKit edits only playlists this app created.
struct LibraryCapabilities: OptionSet, Sendable {
    let rawValue: Int
    static let favoriteSongs        = LibraryCapabilities(rawValue: 1 << 0)
    static let favoriteAlbums       = LibraryCapabilities(rawValue: 1 << 1)
    static let favoriteArtists      = LibraryCapabilities(rawValue: 1 << 2)
    static let createPlaylists      = LibraryCapabilities(rawValue: 1 << 3)
    static let editOwnPlaylists     = LibraryCapabilities(rawValue: 1 << 4)
    static let editForeignPlaylists = LibraryCapabilities(rawValue: 1 << 5)
}

/// Names one playlist across providers. A playlist has no catalog identifier —
/// it does not exist until someone makes it — so it needs a handle.
struct PlaylistHandle: Hashable, Sendable {
    let local: UUID              // ours; stable, survives everything
    let appleLibraryID: String?  // nil = no Apple counterpart (yet, or ever)
}

// MARK: - CloudKit provider records

/// A song, album or artist this kid marked. NEVER a playlist: a playlist is not
/// favorited, it is owned.
@Model
final class FavoriteRecord {
    var id: UUID
    var modifiedAt: Date
    var kid: Kid?

    var catalogID: String        // always an Apple Music catalog identifier
    var itemKind: String         // "song" | "album" | "artist"

    var displayName: String      // copied at write time, never refreshed
    var artworkURL: URL?         // referenced; bytes never stored
    var favoritedAt: Date

    /// "kid"          — tapped in this app
    /// "appleLibrary" — found in the Apple Music library and adopted
    var origin: String
}

/// A playlist the kid owns. Order is the content.
@Model
final class PlaylistRecord {
    var id: UUID
    var modifiedAt: Date
    var kid: Kid?

    var name: String
    var createdAt: Date

    /// The Apple Music library playlist this is the same playlist as.
    ///   nil — no counterpart: never created there, or the provider was not live.
    var appleLibraryID: String?

    /// True ONLY when this app created the Apple counterpart.
    ///
    /// MusicKit refuses to edit a playlist the app did not create and exposes no
    /// way to ask whether it did. Recorded at creation because it is otherwise
    /// unrecoverable: a playlist read back later is indistinguishable from one
    /// Apple made.
    var appleIsOurs: Bool

    var origin: String           // "kid" | "appleLibrary"

    @Relationship(deleteRule: .cascade) var entries: [PlaylistEntryRecord]
}

@Model
final class PlaylistEntryRecord {
    var id: UUID
    var modifiedAt: Date
    var playlist: PlaylistRecord?

    var catalogID: String        // ALWAYS a song
    var displayName: String
    var artworkURL: URL?

    /// 0-based, contiguous after any edit. Gaps are not a supported state.
    var position: Int
    var addedAt: Date
}

// MARK: - Device settings

/// Device-local, deliberately NOT in the CloudKit zone: it describes a device
/// and the Apple Music library on it, not the family. A second device has its
/// own answer, and syncing this would hand it one that is false there.
struct DeviceLibraryState: Codable {
    /// Defaults FALSE — both providers live, which is the case most families
    /// are in and the one the feature is for.
    ///
    /// Onboarding asks before the Apple provider's first read, so this default
    /// governs only the path where that question was never answered.
    var isSharedDevice: Bool
}
```

### Algorithm
**Which providers are live.**

```text
liveProviders() -> [LibraryProvider]

1. if device.isSharedDevice -> [cloudKit]
2. -> [cloudKit, appleMusic]
```

**Favoriting.** One kid-facing verb; a different Apple primitive per kind.

```text
addFavorite(item)

1. if engine.evaluate(item) is .blocked -> refuse, log the block, return
2. cap := item.kind == .song  ? .favoriteSongs
        : item.kind == .album ? .favoriteAlbums
        :                       .favoriteArtists
3. for each provider p in liveProviders() where p.capabilities.contains(cap):
     p.addFavorite(item)
4. cloudKit is AWAITED and a failure is surfaced.
   appleMusic is fire-and-forget and a failure is dropped.
```

Inside the Apple provider the kind picks the primitive: a song or album is **added to the library**; an artist has no library form and takes a favorite alone, if the framework offers one at all.

**Creating a playlist.**

```text
createPlaylist(name, songs)

1. drop any song the engine blocks; if none survive, refuse
2. cloudKit.createPlaylist -> PlaylistRecord(local: UUID, appleIsOurs: false)   // AWAITED
3. if appleMusic live AND supports .createPlaylists:
     3.1 applePlaylist := MusicLibrary.createPlaylist(name:, items: songs)
     3.2 record.appleLibraryID := applePlaylist.id
     3.3 record.appleIsOurs := TRUE       // the only moment this is knowable
4. -> PlaylistHandle(local:, appleLibraryID:)
```

Step 3.3 is why the field exists. MusicKit will not edit a playlist the app did not create and will not say which those are, so a playlist read back later is indistinguishable from one Apple made.

**Editing a playlist.**

```text
addToPlaylist(handle, song) / removeFromPlaylist / renamePlaylist / deletePlaylist

1. if adding: refuse if the engine blocks the song
2. cloudKit: apply, renumber `position` contiguously        // AWAITED
3. if appleMusic live AND handle.appleLibraryID != nil AND record.appleIsOurs:
     apply the same edit there                              // fire-and-forget
   else: skip
```

A playlist with `appleIsOurs == false` still shows and still plays; our copy is edited and Apple's is not. That divergence is stated to the parent in the admin and never to the kid.

**Reading.**

```text
favorites() / playlists()

1. rows := [] ; for each provider p in liveProviders(): rows += try? p.rows()
     // a provider that throws contributes nothing to this pass and is not an error
2. for Apple rows: resolve to catalog identifiers (ISRC / UPC, batched).
     anything that will not resolve is DROPPED, not stored
3. adopt: any Apple row absent from CloudKit -> write a CloudKit record with
     origin: "appleLibrary"      // so it survives the provider going away
4. merged := union by CatalogID (playlists: by PlaylistHandle), most recent first
5. items := catalog.items(for: merged ids)      // batched, cached
6. keep only what the engine allows             // render-time filter
7. -> merged
```

Step 4 is a union. **CloudKit expands what Apple Music returned**; it never contradicts it, prunes it, or pushes back into it. An item present in CloudKit and absent from Apple Music simply appears — which is why a failed Apple write costs the kid nothing visible, and why no reconciliation pass is needed to make the shelf correct.

**Searching the library.**

```text
searchLibrary(term) -> [CatalogItem]

1. entries := favorites() + playlist entries      // already policy-filtered
2. -> entries whose displayName or subtitle matches, case/diacritic-insensitive
```

A local predicate over rows already in hand. `MusicLibrarySearchRequest` is deliberately **not** used: it searches the whole signed-in library rather than the kid's own records.

### Invariants & limits
- **This is the kid's library only.** Nothing here is reachable from the admin, and the admin's existing library seeding (`LibrarySource`, ISRC/UPC matching for allow and deny lists) is neither used by it nor changed by it.
- **Neither a favorite nor a playlist entry is a permission.** Nothing here creates a `PolicyEntry` or changes a verdict. The policy engine remains the single authority.
- **A kid may only favorite, or add to a playlist, what they may currently play.** Every write asks the engine first and refuses a blocked item.
- **Everything read back is filtered at render time, never stored pre-filtered.** A parent may deny tomorrow what the kid favorited today: the row survives, the tile does not.
- **Playlist entries are always songs.** Albums and artists can be favorited but never added to a playlist — what would play is ambiguous, and the player queues songs.
- `isSharedDevice`** is the only input to which providers are live.** False (the default): both. True: CloudKit alone. There is no other gate and no derived trust state.
- `isSharedDevice`** defaults to false, is device-local, and never syncs.** It describes a device and the library on it, not the family.
- **The Apple provider's first read is not issued until onboarding has asked.** The default decides what happens if that question is never answered; it must not decide what happens before it is put.
- **CloudKit is always live.** Every operation therefore has at least one provider, and the feature is complete with Apple Music absent.
- **Callers never name a provider.** Every surface talks to the merged store.
- **A capability a provider lacks is not an error.** It sits that operation out and the others carry it. Only a provider _failing_ something it claims to support is a failure.
- **A read is a union, and CloudKit only ever expands it.** No read prunes, contradicts, or writes back into another provider.
- **Drift between providers is not reconciled.** An item in CloudKit and not in Apple Music stays that way. A deliberate limit, not an oversight: the union makes it invisible where it matters, and healing it is later work if it proves to matter at all.
- **Absence from the Apple Music library never deletes a CloudKit row.**
- **The CloudKit write is awaited and surfaced; the Apple Music write is fire-and-forget.** A heart must not fill on a write that did not land, and a copy that did not reach Apple must never block the kid.
- **Every stored identifier is an Apple Music catalog identifier.** Items read from the Apple Music library are resolved by ISRC and UPC first; anything that will not resolve is dropped rather than stored under a library identifier.
- `appleIsOurs`** is written at creation and never inferred.** MusicKit edits only playlists the app created and exposes no way to ask.
- **An edit is never attempted on a playlist we did not create.**
- **Favorites and playlists are exempt from event retention.** Plays and searches are events and may roll into summaries; these are durable user data, deleted only by the kid or with the kid.
- **Nothing about provider availability is ever shown to a kid.** Capability gaps and provider failures are admin-facing.
- `MusicLibrarySearchRequest`** is not used** for the kid's library search.
- **Artwork bytes are never copied into our storage.** `artworkURL` is a reference; `displayName` is a copied string so a list renders offline.

### Failure & concurrency semantics
**No failure below can take the feature away.** CloudKit is always live, so favorites, playlists and search over them keep working through all of it. What degrades is only whether the kid's library is _also_ a real Apple Music library.

**A provider cannot do something.** Not a failure. The merged store skips it and the others proceed — an artist favorite Apple Music has no primitive for is still a favorite in our records, and the kid sees no difference.

**A provider fails an operation it claims to support.** CloudKit failing is surfaced: the write was the fact, and a filled heart over a failed write is a lie. Apple Music failing is dropped. The item lives in CloudKit, the union puts it on the shelf anyway, and the only cost is that it is not in the kid's Apple Music library. **There is no retry and no queue** — see the note on drift below.

**Apple Music unavailable.** No subscription, iCloud Music Library off, no network, authorization revoked mid-session: all the same shape. The provider throws or returns nothing, contributes nothing to that pass, and the CloudKit rows render alone. None of these is modelled as a distinct state, because none of them changes what the app should do.

**A library read fails.** Treated as an empty Apple library for that pass. No adoption, no deletion, and nothing pushed — there is nothing to push, because reads never write back into a provider.

**Resolution failure.** A library item whose ISRC or UPC finds no catalog match is dropped from that read and never stored. Not an error, not shown to the kid, counted in the admin — the rate is open research question 2 and this is the first feature that depends on it at runtime.

**Drift is a known, accepted, permanent-until-addressed condition.** Two libraries can disagree: a failed write, a device that was shared when the favorite was made, a song the kid removed in the Music app. None of it is repaired. The union means the kid's shelf is right regardless — CloudKit holds everything — so drift costs only the completeness of the Apple-side copy. If that turns out to matter, reconciliation is a later pass over the same seam and needs no schema change to add.

**Playlist divergence** is the one case where the two disagree about _content_ rather than completeness: a playlist with `appleIsOurs == false` accepts edits in our copy and silently not in Apple's. Permanent rather than transient, so the admin states it plainly.

**Offline.** No download story exists under the MusicKit terms, so offline means no playback regardless. The lists still render — `displayName` and `artworkURL` are copied at write time precisely so they can.

**Conflict and concurrency.** `FavoriteRecord` is keyed by `(kid, catalogID, itemKind)` and writes are upserts, so the same favorite arriving twice — tapped twice, or adopted while being tapped — collapses to one row. Playlist `position` is renumbered contiguously after every edit rather than left sparse, so two racing edits produce a consistent order rather than a gap. Under CloudKit sync in v2, two devices asserting the same favorite converge last-writer-wins on `modifiedAt`, correct for set membership. An unfavorite racing an adoption is the one real conflict: the unfavorite wins, being the only one of the two a person did deliberately.

**Provisional results.** A verdict on an item whose ancestry has not resolved is provisional, as everywhere: deny fails open, allow-only fails closed. The player re-checks immediately before playback regardless, which is what makes a playlist built weeks ago safe to press play on.

### Data dependencies
Four inputs. Two are local and immediate; two arrive after launch with a real window before they do.

**The policy engine** — in process, synchronous, no window. Rebuilt when the kid's policy changes. Consulted on every write and every read. Nothing here is judged by anything else.

**CloudKit provider rows** — local SwiftData, available on the first frame. This is why there is no meaningful loading state: names and artwork URLs were copied at write time, so the shelf draws before any network call resolves anything. `DeviceLibraryState` is read synchronously alongside them and never syncs.

**Authorization and subscription state** — `MusicAuthorization.request()` once, then `MusicSubscription.current` and `subscriptionUpdates` for the session. The Apple provider needs both, and authorization can be revoked in Settings mid-session. Neither is consulted to decide whether the provider is _live_ — `isSharedDevice` alone does that — but either can make it return nothing, which is handled as a provider contributing nothing rather than as a state.

**The Apple Music library** — `MusicLibraryRequest`, requiring authorization _and_ `hasCloudLibraryEnabled`. Its items arrive as library identifiers and are **not usable until resolved to catalog identifiers** by a second batched request on ISRC and UPC. Between those two steps items are only partly known, and nothing is written, judged or displayed in that window.

### The dependency this feature is least sure of

The library-to-catalog resolution rate. Open research question 2 asks whether ISRC and UPC are populated often enough for library seeding to be worth offering; until now a poor rate meant an optional admin shortcut discarded more. Here it means a kid's own library reads back incomplete — they added a song in the Music app and it is not here.

That failure is quiet and reads as a bug in us, which is why the admin counts discards. It is bounded, though: it affects only what the Apple provider contributes to a read. Nothing the kid does in this app depends on it, because everything the kid does lands in CloudKit first.

### A dependency that may not exist

Whether MusicKit Swift exposes favoriting at all, for any kind. Adding a song or album to the library is documented and certain; favoriting is not, and artists have no library form to fall back on. If it turns out to be Apple Music API only, the provider reaches it through `MusicDataRequest`, which carries the user token to arbitrary endpoints — the seam absorbs that and no caller learns of it. See Open questions this opens.

### Migration & existing data
**Nothing to migrate: none of this exists.** There is no favorites, likes, hearts or playlist concept anywhere in `FamilyStore`, `CatalogKit` or the app, and nothing in the wiki describes one. `FavoriteRecord`, `PlaylistRecord` and `PlaylistEntryRecord` are new models in the existing named custom CloudKit zone, and every existing kid simply has none of them.

**The admin's library seeding is not migrated, wrapped or refactored.** `LibrarySource` and its ISRC/UPC matching stay exactly as they are. They are a parent's shortcut for building allow and deny lists and have nothing to do with the kid's library beyond both involving the word.

Three things do meet what already exists, and each is a decision rather than a no-op.

**Existing plays are not backfilled into favorites.** The data is right there in `PlayEventRecord` and seeding from most-played would look generous. It would be wrong. A favorite is something a kid _said_, and manufacturing a hundred from a play log would put items on their shelf they never chose and then invite them to unfavorite things they never favorited. The library starts empty, and that emptiness is honest.

**A pre-existing Apple Music library is adopted on the first read**, becoming `origin: "appleLibrary"` rows. For a kid with their own account that is the whole point — it is their library and always was, and adopting it is the feature working on day one rather than starting them at zero.

It is also the one moment this feature can go badly wrong, because the same pass on a parent's account pulls an adult library onto a child's shelf. Three things stand between those outcomes, and none of them is the default:

1. **Onboarding asks before the first read happens** (see Invariants & limits). The parent answers the question while there is still nothing adopted, which is what makes `isSharedDevice = false` safe as a default rather than merely convenient.
2. **The policy engine judges every adopted row at render time.** Explicit and unrated content is filtered on a level 2 kid's shelf exactly as it is everywhere else, and shows up in the parent's report as blocks.
3. **Adopted rows carry **`origin: "appleLibrary"`, so the report can say which of a kid's favorites they chose and which arrived with the account. A shelf that filled itself is visible as such rather than looking like a very busy week.

**"Yours" changes meaning on the level 1 home screen.** It currently labels the parent's allow list. Once a kid has favorites and playlists, that word describes those, and the allow list needs another — "From your grown-up", or similar. A visible-string change with no stored data behind it, but it lands on the screen a level 1 kid sees most, so it ships with the shelf.

**Retention must learn about these tables before retention ships.** Open question 6 weighs a 90-day rolling window on child event data. Whatever is chosen, these are **not** events and must be exempt (see Invariants & limits). A sweep written against "child data older than 90 days" would delete a kid's playlists silently, months later, and they are the records in the whole store with the most work in them.

### Where favorites and playlists appear
**The heart.** On a song row it sits at the leading edge of the trailing controls, beside the play button; on a tile it goes in the text area. **Never on the artwork** — the app's standing rule is clipping yes, compositing never, and a heart burned onto Apple's pixels is exactly what that rule forbids. Filled and outline, no count, no animation a kid has to sit through.

It appears on songs, albums and artists alike, and reads the same on all three even though the primitive underneath differs by kind.

**Search results.** Every row and tile shows whether it is already favorited — a local set lookup against rows in memory, costing nothing and needing no request. The search screen gains no fourth tab: Artists, Songs and Albums are searches of the catalog, and a "Favorites" tab that searched something else entirely would be the odd one out.

**The home screen.** A "Yours" shelf holding favorites, and a playlists shelf beside it, both built the way Recent already is: resolved from stored identifiers in one batched request and filtered at render time. In level 1 these sit alongside the parent's list, which now has its own name.

**Playlists.** A kid makes one from the now-playing screen or from a song's row, names it with the keyboard, and reorders by dragging. Songs are added from anywhere a song appears. Playing one queues its songs in order — and the player re-checks every track immediately before it plays, which is what makes a playlist built weeks ago safe to press play on today.

A playlist name is free text a child typed. It syncs to their Apple Music library and appears in the parent's report, and both of those are worth saying out loud before the field is built rather than after.

**Library search.** A local predicate over merged rows, reached from the shelf rather than from the main search field. A kid with forty favorites does not need to search them; a kid with four hundred does, and that kid exists a year in.

**The parent's report.** A favorite is a stronger signal than a play — a play can be an accident and a favorite cannot — so favorites and playlists get their own lines, with one-tap widening to the allow list.

### Open questions this opens
Three, and **none of them gates the design**. Each changes only what the Apple Music provider turns out to be capable of, and a capability that provider lacks is one CloudKit still has (see Invariants & limits). They are measurements that tune behaviour at the margins, not decisions the architecture waits on. All should reach _Open Questions and Research Tasks_ alongside the existing numbered list.

**1. Does MusicKit Swift expose favoriting at all, and for which kinds?** Adding a song or album to the library is documented and certain. _Favoriting_ is not, and it is the only primitive an artist has — there is no "add artist to library" in Apple Music. The Apple Music API has ratings endpoints (`/v1/me/ratings/…`, love and dislike) and newer favorites endpoints, but whether the Swift framework surfaces either is unverified. If it does not, the provider reaches them through `MusicDataRequest`, which carries the user token to arbitrary endpoints. Whatever the answer, it lands as capability flags: `favoriteArtists` may simply be absent, and artist favorites then live in CloudKit alone.

**2. What is the real ISRC/UPC resolution rate?** Existing research question 2, promoted from _is library seeding worth offering_ to _does the kid's own library read back completely_. A poor rate used to mean an optional admin shortcut discarded more; now it means a kid adds a song in the Music app and it is not here. Bounded, though: it affects only what the Apple provider contributes to a read, never what is stored, because everything the kid does in this app lands in CloudKit first.

**3. Can a playlist we created be recognised as ours after a reinstall?** `appleIsOurs` lives in the CloudKit zone, so it survives a reinstall on the same family account — but a playlist created before this app existed, or on a device whose records were lost, reads as foreign forever and quietly stops accepting edits. Whether MusicKit has gained any way to ask since WWDC22 is worth one look before accepting that as permanent.

### Not a question, but worth stating

**This sends a child's taste data to Apple.** "Nothing leaves the device" is a legal position in CLAUDE.md aimed at our servers and third-party analytics, and Apple under the family's own account is neither. But it is a change in kind from an app that until now kept a child's listening entirely local, and it belongs in onboarding in the same breath as the shared-device toggle rather than being discovered later. The licence permits the use — §3.3.6(D) allows user metadata for a function "clearly disclosed to end users and directly relevant to the use of Your Application" — and _clearly disclosed_ is a condition, not a description.

_Not reviewed._

_None._

# What We Know About MusicKit

**Status:** active

## Body
Verified against Apple's docs and license terms as of July 2026. These are the facts that shape the design. Anything still unknown lives in Open Questions and Research Tasks.

## The basics work in our favor

- `ApplicationMusicPlayer` streams the full Apple Music catalog _inside our app_, with its own queue, separate from the Music app's state. It also keeps playing in the background if we set the audio background mode. This is exactly the primitive we need.
- Native apps don't need a server or a developer token. Enable the MusicKit capability on the App ID and MusicKit handles tokens automatically. A first version can be entirely client-side.
- Authorization is a normal permission prompt via `MusicAuthorization.request()`.
- Playback needs an active Apple Music subscription on the signed-in account. Check `MusicSubscription.current.canPlayCatalogContent` before promising anything, and `canBecomeSubscriber` if we want to offer a signup.
- Under Family Sharing, each kid can have their own Apple Account (yes, under 13) with their own library, history, and recommendations, all covered by one Apple Music Family plan. That means a kid's listening doesn't pollute the parent's recommendations — important, and it's the setup we should assume.

## Platform floors

| Thing | iOS | macOS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MusicKit, `MusicSubscription`, `contentRating` | 15.0+ | 12.0+ |
| `ApplicationMusicPlayer` | 15.0+ | **14.0+** |
| Family Controls / Screen Time API | 15.0+ | Catalyst only, no native Mac |

The macOS 14 floor on the player is the notable one. Sonoma or newer for the Mac app, no way around it if we want in-app playback.

## Explicit detection is thinner than you'd hope

This is the single most important finding for level 2, and it's worse than expected.

- `ContentRating` has exactly two cases: `.clean` and `.explicit`. The property is optional, and `nil` means "no rating available" — not "safe." So "non-explicit" is a three-state problem, not a boolean, and we have to decide what to do with unrated tracks.
- Song and Album both have `contentRating`. **Playlist does not.** A playlist has to be judged track by track, and its tracks can change under us at any time.
- **Search has no content filter at all.** `MusicCatalogSearchRequest` exposes only `term`, `types`, `limit`, `offset`, and `includeTopResults`. Every bit of filtering is ours, client-side, after the results come back. That means holes in result pages and over-fetching to compensate.
- A rating tells you about lyrics, not about themes. A clean-rated song can still be about something a parent wouldn't pick. Level 2 is a filter, not a guarantee, and we should describe it that way.

## Screen Time interacts with playback, unpredictably

Two separate systems can block explicit playback underneath us: the device's Screen Time content restriction (Music, Podcasts & News set to "Clean") and Apple Music's own Parental Controls in account settings. When either is on, third-party MusicKit playback of an explicit track fails.

- MusicKit JS developers report a hard `CONTENT_RESTRICTED` error. Apple couldn't reproduce it on a filed Feedback (FB12353357) and it's still open.
- On Mac, tracks with `contentRating == .explicit` have been reported to fail with "Failed to prepare to play" (`MPMusicPlayerControllerErrorDomain` 6) while the same tracks play on iOS.

Read both ways: it's a useful second layer of defense we get for free, and it's a source of confusing failures we'll have to handle gracefully. Either way we cannot rely on it — our own filtering has to be the real gate. It also means we need clear error handling for "blocked by something outside this app," or parents will report it as our bug.

## License terms that constrain the product

From the Apple Developer Program License Agreement, section 3.3.6(D), plus the MusicKit terms. Paraphrased — read the current agreement directly before making business decisions on these.

- Full songs must be enabled for playback. No clipping or previewing as a safety mechanism.
- The user must initiate playback and have standard controls: play, pause, skip.
- Content plays only as rendered by the MusicKit APIs. No downloading, uploading, or modifying.
- Artwork and music text can only appear alongside playback or playlist management, not on their own.
- User metadata such as playlists and favorites may only be used for a clearly disclosed purpose directly relevant to the app.
- **You may not require payment for, or indirectly monetize access to, the Apple Music service, including through in-app purchase, advertising, or requesting user info.**

That last one needs a real answer before we pick a business model. A paid parental-control app that only works with the user's own Apple Music subscription is probably fine, but "probably" isn't good enough to build on.

## Kids Category rules, if we go there

- Pick one age band: 5 and under, 6 to 8, or 9 to 11.
- No third-party analytics. No third-party ads.
- No personally identifiable info or device info to third parties, including from the adult section, without explicit parental consent.
- Parental gates required before in-app purchase or any link out of the app. For pre-readers, gates need voiceover prompts.
- The rules are sticky. Once customers expect Kids Category behavior, later updates must keep meeting it even if we deselect the category.

Worth noting: this app is arguably for the parent, used by the kid. We may be better off rated 4+ outside the Kids Category, which keeps the analytics and gating rules from binding us. That's a decision, not a given.

## Family Controls needs Apple's permission, and lead time

- Entitlement is `com.apple.developer.family-controls`. Development works immediately; shipping to TestFlight or the App Store does not.
- Distribution requires a separate manual request to Apple, per bundle ID, plus one for every Screen Time extension we ship.
- Reported turnaround runs from a few business days to several weeks. If we want it, request early.
- Apple looks for a genuine parental-control use case and specifically checks you're not harvesting usage data for advertising or profiling. Our reporting feature needs to be framed carefully.
- Once authorized, the framework blocks the child from deleting the app or signing out of iCloud, which is the actual tamper resistance we'd be buying.

## Measured on a device, not read in a doc

Everything above this line is desk research. Everything in this section is something we had wrong until a real device said otherwise, on the first run against the real Apple Music API in July 2026. Each one cost a working build, and none of them could have been caught here: the test stubs serve whatever they are asked for, `swift build` targets macOS, and MusicKit in the simulator refuses playback outright with `MPMusicPlayerController is not available on the simulator`.

### Search caps `limit` at 25

Asking for more is a hard failure, not a clamped page:

```text
GET /v1/catalog/us/search?term=Punch&types=songs&limit=75&offset=0

400  code 40005  Invalid Parameter Value
"Value must be an integer less than or equal to 25, but was: 75"
source: .parameter("limit")
```

This breaks the over-fetch strategy as originally designed. The loop asked for the caller's limit times an over-fetch multiplier of 3, under a page ceiling of 100 — so a perfectly ordinary search for 25 songs asked for 75 and every single search failed.

- **Over-fetching has to happen by paging, not by asking for a bigger page.** Once the caller's limit reaches 25 the multiplier has no room left at all, and the only way to compensate for filtering holes is more requests at increasing offsets. The multiplier still earns its keep at smaller limits, where one request can cover the need.
- `hasMore` must be judged against the _clamped_ limit, not the asked-for one. Judged against the request, a full page of 25 reads as "fewer than the 75 I wanted, so the catalog is exhausted" and paging stops after one request — turning a loud 400 into a silent truncation that looks like a search legitimately finding little.
- The cap is specific to search. Other endpoints allow more.

### Relationship items can arrive with empty identifiers

Resolving ancestry on real search results logs this, freely and often:

```text
No catalogID, libraryID, or deviceLocalID was found from underlying
identifier set <MPIdentifierSet EMPTY>. A MusicIdentifierSet with empty
string, for type MusicItemTypeValue(type: Album, rawValue: "Album"), is
being used.
```

An album or artist reached through a song's relationship may have an empty identifier. Storing that as an ancestor is worse than storing nothing: it matches no real album, every affected song shares the one identifier, and — the dangerous part — the item then _looks_ like it has lineage. The provisional-verdict rule keys off ancestry being empty, so a bogus entry turns a guess into what reads as a resolved fact. Empty identifiers are dropped rather than stored.

Whether ancestry resolves _at all_ on real results is a separate question this log cannot answer — it does not distinguish harmless noise from lineage silently failing to arrive. See Open Questions and Research Tasks.

### The MusicKit capability cannot be verified from a build

MusicKit is an App Service on the App ID, not an entitlement. It never appears in the provisioning profile, so a cleanly signed build proves the bundle identifier matches and signing works, and says nothing whatsoever about whether MusicKit is enabled. The only proof is a catalog request that comes back — a well-formed API error counts, an authorization failure does not.

### The account-store entitlement error is noise

Every launch logs this, several times:

```text
<ICUserIdentityStoreACAccountBackend> Failed to initialize active account,
error=Error Domain=ICError Code=-7013 "Client is not entitled to access
account store"

[ICUserIdentityStore] Failed to fetch local store account with error:
Error Domain=ICError Code=-7013 ...
```

`ICUserIdentityStore` belongs to the private iTunesCloud framework, and the account store it wants needs `com.apple.accounts.appleaccount.fullaccess` — an entitlement only Apple's own apps hold. Every third-party MusicKit app logs this. It does not affect authorization, subscription state, search or playback: the session that produced these lines was searching and playing fine.

Written down only because it reads exactly like the entitlement problem that _would_ explain a broken MusicKit setup, and chasing it costs an afternoon. If subscription state, storefront or account identity ever look wrong, this is the first log to re-examine — but on its own it is not evidence of anything.

## Sources

- [MusicKit overview](https://developer.apple.com/musickit/)
- [ApplicationMusicPlayer](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/applicationmusicplayer) and [MusicSubscription](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/musicsubscription)
- [ContentRating](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/contentrating), [Song](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/song), [Album](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/album), [Playlist](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/playlist)
- [MusicCatalogSearchRequest](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/musiccatalogsearchrequest)
- [Apple Developer Program License Agreement](https://developer.apple.com/support/terms/apple-developer-program-license-agreement/) (section 3.3.6(D))
- [App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/) and [The Kids Category](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/kids-apps/)
- [Family Controls](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/familycontrols) and [Configuring Family Controls](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/configuring-family-controls)
- [How Family Sharing works](https://support.apple.com/en-us/105062)
- [CONTENT_RESTRICTED forum thread](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/731897)

## What the licence says about artwork and content

Verbatim from the **Apple Developer Program License Agreement** §3.3.6(D) "MusicKit", English-UK edition, page 32, read 27 July 2026. Fetched as PDF from developer.apple.com and text-extracted rather than paraphrased, because the exact wording is what the argument turns on.

> You agree not to call the MusicKit APIs or use MusicKit JS (or otherwise attempt to gain information through the MusicKit APIs or MusicKit JS) for purposes unrelated to facilitating access to Your end users' Apple Music subscriptions. If You access the MusicKit APIs or MusicKit JS, then You must follow the Apple Music Identity Guidelines.
>
> If You choose to offer music playback through the MusicKit APIs or MusicKit JS, full songs must be enabled for playback, and users must initiate playback and be able to navigate playback using standard media controls, such as "play", "pause" and "skip", and You agree to not misrepresent the functionality of these controls;
>
> You may not, and You may not permit Your end users to, download, upload or modify any MusicKit Content and MusicKit Content cannot be synchronised with any other content, unless otherwise permitted by Apple in the Documentation;
>
> You may play MusicKit Content only as rendered by the MusicKit APIs or MusicKit JS and only as permitted in the Documentation (e.g. album art and music-related text from the MusicKit API may not be used separately from music playback or managing playlists);
>
> Metadata from users (such as playlists and favourites) may only be used to provide a service or function that is clearly disclosed to end users and that is directly relevant to the use of Your Application, website or web application, as determined at Apple's sole discretion

**The operative word is "modify", and nothing defines it.** No clause names overlays, cropping or masking. The exposure is that a play badge laid over artwork obscures part of it and a circular mask removes part of it, and both are arguable modifications of MusicKit Content. This is not settled either way, so the app draws its own line and stays on one side of it: _clipping yes, compositing never_. The shape of the frame is ours; what the frame contains is Apple's and nothing of ours is ever drawn on top of it.

**What follows for the kid player's tiles.** Every kind distinction is drawn outside the artwork: a card behind the tile for anything that opens, a caret at the trailing edge of the line naming the kind, a play glyph beside the title for songs, and the kind word in that line. The artwork carries none of it.

- **Artists are masked to a circle, everything else to a rounded rectangle.** A circle crops harder than a rounded rectangle, so it is further along the clipping line rather than across a new one, and it is what the Music app itself does for artists — the convention a kid will have met in every other music app. This and the corner radius are the only places the app interprets "modify" rather than simply avoiding it.
- **Nothing is ever composited onto artwork.** No play badge, no lock, no overlay of any kind. A badge on the artwork was the first treatment considered and was dropped for this reason; the play glyph lives beside the title instead.
- **Placeholder glyphs are ours, not Apple's**. They appear only when there is no artwork — common for artists — so nothing is ever drawn over a real image.
- **Artwork bytes are still never copied into our storage**, which the same clause forbids outright. Only the URL is stored.

**The Apple Music Identity Guidelines do not mention album artwork at all.** All 63 sections cover Apple's own badges, lockups, icons, Shazam assets and marketing copy. This is worth writing down because it looks relevant and is not: a search for Apple Music "badge" rules returns "never change the badge artwork in any way", which is about the _Listen on Apple Music_ button and says nothing about a play glyph on a tile. The two meanings of "badge" are easy to conflate and the guidelines are incorporated into the licence by reference, so the mistake looks well-sourced.

### Artwork is cached in memory only — and `AsyncImage` was not

The clause above forbids _downloading_ MusicKit Content, and the standing rule is that only the artwork URL is stored. **SwiftUI's AsyncImage breaks that rule by default.** It loads through `URLSession.shared`, which uses `URLCache.shared` — and that has a disk capacity as well as a memory one. Every cover a kid scrolled past was being written to disk by the URL loading system, with no code of ours asking for it.

This one is read from Apple's documented defaults, not measured on a device — it sits above the measured line for that reason. That `URLCache.shared` is disk-backed is not in doubt; the on-disk footprint in this app is unquantified, and a probe that reads the cache directory after a scroll would settle it.

What the app does instead: `ArtworkCache` holds decoded images in an `NSCache`, behind a session built from `URLSessionConfiguration.ephemeral` with `urlCache` set to nil — no HTTP cache at all, nothing on the filesystem, and eviction under memory pressure for free. **The same change fixed artwork intermittently never appearing**: `AsyncImage` keeps nothing between appearances, shows its placeholder for a failure as well as a load, and never asks twice, so one lost request among two dozen tiles left a permanent grey square.

### Indirect monetisation — verbatim text for open question 4

The clause behind research question 4, from the same section. It narrows the question without settling it: the prohibition attaches to monetising _access to the Apple Music service_, not to charging for an application generally.

> You agree not to require payment for or indirectly monetise access to the Apple Music service (e.g. in-app purchase, advertising, requesting user info) through Your use of the MusicKit APIs, MusicKit JS or otherwise in any way.

**Still unanswered, and still blocking business-model decisions.** Whether a paid app that charges for the sandbox rather than for Apple Music falls inside "otherwise in any way" is a question for a lawyer, not for reading. What has changed is that the wording is now in hand rather than being recalled second-hand.

## Reading the parent's own library: playlists and artists

Established July 2026, while building parent suggestions. Everything below **compiles against the real MusicKit SDK** on macOS — which is a stronger claim than "recalled from the documentation" and a weaker one than "seen working". The MusicKit capability is still not enabled on the App ID, so none of it has run against a real account.

- `MusicLibraryRequest<Playlist>` and `MusicLibraryRequest<Artist>` both exist and take `.limit`, alongside the `<Song>` and `<Album>` requests already in use. Library seeding was song-and-album only because those are the kinds with codes, not because the other requests were missing.
- `MusicLibraryRequest<Playlist>` accepts `filter(matching: \.id, equalTo: MusicItemID(...))`, which is how one playlist is refetched by identifier after crossing out of CatalogKit as a value.
- A library `Playlist` exposes `name`, `curatorName`, `artwork`, `kind` and `tracks`, and `.with([.tracks])` loads them the same way it does for a catalog playlist. `tracks` is a collection of `Track`, so music videos have to be filtered out — the same `compactMap` that `children(of:)` already does.
- `Playlist.kind` is `nil` for a playlist the account holder made themselves. Every case of `Playlist.Kind` names something Apple produced, `personalMix` included — that one is a mix Apple built _for_ them, which is not the same thing. **Unverified:** whether a nil kind really is the only marker of an own-made playlist. It decides only a label a parent reads, never what is resolved.
- **There is still no way to get a catalog identifier for a library item.** No documented property returns one, and for a playlist there is nothing to return — nobody published it. The `PlayParameters`-to-JSON trick that circulates is undocumented, its keys are version-dependent, and it is deliberately not used here.

That last point forces two things, and both turn out cheaper than the missing identifier suggests. **A playlist is snapshotted track by track** through the ISRC path that already existed, and stored under a local UUID — so the catalog playlist identifier is never needed, not even for one of Apple's. **An artist is derived rather than matched**: `resolveToCatalog` already requests `[.albums, .artists]`, so a resolved song arrives carrying its catalog artist, and naming a library artist means resolving a sample of their songs and reading it off the results. No new matching rule, and no new request shape.

`song.artists.first` is not good enough to derive from on its own. It is right most of the time and wrong in exactly the cases a family library is full of: a track with a guest credit names the guest, a soundtrack names whoever opened it, a ripped compilation names “Various Artists”. So it is a majority vote over roughly ten songs, dropping empty identifiers first, that **refuses rather than guesses** when nothing clears the bar. The asymmetry is worth stating: a suggested artist is an allowed artist, so a wrong answer here hands a child a catalogue nobody chose — where a refusal costs the parent one catalog search.

One side effect worth noticing: the suggest-a-playlist confirm screen shows the parent “34 of 39 songs matched” before they commit, which makes the ISRC hit rate on a real library something the app reports every time it is used rather than something a hand-run probe has to answer once. That is open research question 2, measured continuously, as soon as the capability is enabled.

Apple couldn't reproduce it on a filed Feedback (FB12353357) and it's still open.\n- On Mac, tracks with `contentRating == .explicit` have been reported to fail with \"Failed to prepare to play\" (`MPMusicPlayerControllerErrorDomain` 6) while the same tracks play on iOS.\n\nRead both ways: it's a useful second layer of defense we get for free, and it's a source of confusing failures we'll have to handle gracefully. Either way we cannot rely on it — our own filtering has to be the real gate. It also means we need clear error handling for \"blocked by something outside this app,\" or parents will report it as our bug.\n\n## License terms that constrain the product\n\nFrom the Apple Developer Program License Agreement, section 3.3.6(D), plus the MusicKit terms. Paraphrased — read the current agreement directly before making business decisions on these.\n\n- Full songs must be enabled for playback. No clipping or previewing as a safety mechanism.\n- The user must initiate playback and have standard controls: play, pause, skip.\n- Content plays only as rendered by the MusicKit APIs. No downloading, uploading, or modifying.\n- Artwork and music text can only appear alongside playback or playlist management, not on their own.\n- User metadata such as playlists and favorites may only be used for a clearly disclosed purpose directly relevant to the app.\n- **You may not require payment for, or indirectly monetize access to, the Apple Music service, including through in-app purchase, advertising, or requesting user info.**\n\nThat last one needs a real answer before we pick a business model. A paid parental-control app that only works with the user's own Apple Music subscription is probably fine, but \"probably\" isn't good enough to build on.\n\n## Kids Category rules, if we go there\n\n- Pick one age band: 5 and under, 6 to 8, or 9 to 11.\n- No third-party analytics. No third-party ads.\n- No personally identifiable info or device info to third parties, including from the adult section, without explicit parental consent.\n- Parental gates required before in-app purchase or any link out of the app. For pre-readers, gates need voiceover prompts.\n- The rules are sticky. Once customers expect Kids Category behavior, later updates must keep meeting it even if we deselect the category.\n\nWorth noting: this app is arguably for the parent, used by the kid. We may be better off rated 4+ outside the Kids Category, which keeps the analytics and gating rules from binding us. That's a decision, not a given.\n\n## Family Controls needs Apple's permission, and lead time\n\n- Entitlement is `com.apple.developer.family-controls`. Development works immediately; shipping to TestFlight or the App Store does not.\n- Distribution requires a separate manual request to Apple, per bundle ID, plus one for every Screen Time extension we ship.\n- Reported turnaround runs from a few business days to several weeks. If we want it, request early.\n- Apple looks for a genuine parental-control use case and specifically checks you're not harvesting usage data for advertising or profiling. Our reporting feature needs to be framed carefully.\n- Once authorized, the framework blocks the child from deleting the app or signing out of iCloud, which is the actual tamper resistance we'd be buying.\n\n## Measured on a device, not read in a doc\n\nEverything above this line is desk research. Everything in this section is something we had wrong until a real device said otherwise, on the first run against the real Apple Music API in July 2026. Each one cost a working build, and none of them could have been caught here: the test stubs serve whatever they are asked for, `swift build` targets macOS, and MusicKit in the simulator refuses playback outright with `MPMusicPlayerController is not available on the simulator`.\n\n### Search caps `limit` at 25\n\nAsking for more is a hard failure, not a clamped page:\n\n```text\nGET /v1/catalog/us/search?term=Punch&types=songs&limit=75&offset=0\n\n400  code 40005  Invalid Parameter Value\n\"Value must be an integer less than or equal to 25, but was: 75\"\nsource: .parameter(\"limit\")\n```\n\nThis breaks the over-fetch strategy as originally designed. The loop asked for the caller's limit times an over-fetch multiplier of 3, under a page ceiling of 100 — so a perfectly ordinary search for 25 songs asked for 75 and every single search failed.\n\n- **Over-fetching has to happen by paging, not by asking for a bigger page.** Once the caller's limit reaches 25 the multiplier has no room left at all, and the only way to compensate for filtering holes is more requests at increasing offsets. The multiplier still earns its keep at smaller limits, where one request can cover the need.\n- `hasMore` must be judged against the _clamped_ limit, not the asked-for one. Judged against the request, a full page of 25 reads as \"fewer than the 75 I wanted, so the catalog is exhausted\" and paging stops after one request — turning a loud 400 into a silent truncation that looks like a search legitimately finding little.\n- The cap is specific to search. Other endpoints allow more.\n\n### Relationship items can arrive with empty identifiers\n\nResolving ancestry on real search results logs this, freely and often:\n\n```text\nNo catalogID, libraryID, or deviceLocalID was found from underlying\nidentifier set <MPIdentifierSet EMPTY>. A MusicIdentifierSet with empty\nstring, for type MusicItemTypeValue(type: Album, rawValue: \"Album\"), is\nbeing used.\n```\n\nAn album or artist reached through a song's relationship may have an empty identifier. Storing that as an ancestor is worse than storing nothing: it matches no real album, every affected song shares the one identifier, and — the dangerous part — the item then _looks_ like it has lineage. The provisional-verdict rule keys off ancestry being empty, so a bogus entry turns a guess into what reads as a resolved fact. Empty identifiers are dropped rather than stored.\n\nWhether ancestry resolves _at all_ on real results is a separate question this log cannot answer — it does not distinguish harmless noise from lineage silently failing to arrive. See Open Questions and Research Tasks.\n\n### The MusicKit capability cannot be verified from a build\n\nMusicKit is an App Service on the App ID, not an entitlement. It never appears in the provisioning profile, so a cleanly signed build proves the bundle identifier matches and signing works, and says nothing whatsoever about whether MusicKit is enabled. The only proof is a catalog request that comes back — a well-formed API error counts, an authorization failure does not.\n\n### The account-store entitlement error is noise\n\nEvery launch logs this, several times:\n\n```text\n<ICUserIdentityStoreACAccountBackend> Failed to initialize active account,\nerror=Error Domain=ICError Code=-7013 \"Client is not entitled to access\naccount store\"\n\n[ICUserIdentityStore] Failed to fetch local store account with error:\nError Domain=ICError Code=-7013 ...\n```\n\n`ICUserIdentityStore` belongs to the private iTunesCloud framework, and the account store it wants needs `com.apple.accounts.appleaccount.fullaccess` — an entitlement only Apple's own apps hold. Every third-party MusicKit app logs this. It does not affect authorization, subscription state, search or playback: the session that produced these lines was searching and playing fine.\n\nWritten down only because it reads exactly like the entitlement problem that _would_ explain a broken MusicKit setup, and chasing it costs an afternoon. If subscription state, storefront or account identity ever look wrong, this is the first log to re-examine — but on its own it is not evidence of anything.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [MusicKit overview](https://developer.apple.com/musickit/)\n- [ApplicationMusicPlayer](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/applicationmusicplayer) and [MusicSubscription](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/musicsubscription)\n- [ContentRating](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/contentrating), [Song](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/song), [Album](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/album), [Playlist](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/playlist)\n- [MusicCatalogSearchRequest](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/musickit/musiccatalogsearchrequest)\n- [Apple Developer Program License Agreement](https://developer.apple.com/support/terms/apple-developer-program-license-agreement/) (section 3.3.6(D))\n- [App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/) and [The Kids Category](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/kids-apps/)\n- [Family Controls](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/familycontrols) and [Configuring Family Controls](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/configuring-family-controls)\n- [How Family Sharing works](https://support.apple.com/en-us/105062)\n- [CONTENT_RESTRICTED forum thread](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/731897)\n\n## What the licence says about artwork and content\n\nVerbatim from the **Apple Developer Program License Agreement** §3.3.6(D) \"MusicKit\", English-UK edition, page 32, read 27 July 2026. Fetched as PDF from developer.apple.com and text-extracted rather than paraphrased, because the exact wording is what the argument turns on.\n\n> You agree not to call the MusicKit APIs or use MusicKit JS (or otherwise attempt to gain information through the MusicKit APIs or MusicKit JS) for purposes unrelated to facilitating access to Your end users' Apple Music subscriptions. If You access the MusicKit APIs or MusicKit JS, then You must follow the Apple Music Identity Guidelines.\n>\n> If You choose to offer music playback through the MusicKit APIs or MusicKit JS, full songs must be enabled for playback, and users must initiate playback and be able to navigate playback using standard media controls, such as \"play\", \"pause\" and \"skip\", and You agree to not misrepresent the functionality of these controls;\n>\n> You may not, and You may not permit Your end users to, download, upload or modify any MusicKit Content and MusicKit Content cannot be synchronised with any other content, unless otherwise permitted by Apple in the Documentation;\n>\n> You may play MusicKit Content only as rendered by the MusicKit APIs or MusicKit JS and only as permitted in the Documentation (e.g. album art and music-related text from the MusicKit API may not be used separately from music playback or managing playlists);\n>\n> Metadata from users (such as playlists and favourites) may only be used to provide a service or function that is clearly disclosed to end users and that is directly relevant to the use of Your Application, website or web application, as determined at Apple's sole discretion\n\n**The operative word is \"modify\", and nothing defines it.** No clause names overlays, cropping or masking. The exposure is that a play badge laid over artwork obscures part of it and a circular mask removes part of it, and both are arguable modifications of MusicKit Content. This is not settled either way, so the app draws its own line and stays on one side of it: _clipping yes, compositing never_. The shape of the frame is ours; what the frame contains is Apple's and nothing of ours is ever drawn on top of it.\n\n**What follows for the kid player's tiles.** Every kind distinction is drawn outside the artwork: a card behind the tile for anything that opens, a caret at the trailing edge of the line naming the kind, a play glyph beside the title for songs, and the kind word in that line. The artwork carries none of it.\n\n- **Artists are masked to a circle, everything else to a rounded rectangle.** A circle crops harder than a rounded rectangle, so it is further along the clipping line rather than across a new one, and it is what the Music app itself does for artists — the convention a kid will have met in every other music app. This and the corner radius are the only places the app interprets \"modify\" rather than simply avoiding it.\n- **Nothing is ever composited onto artwork.** No play badge, no lock, no overlay of any kind. A badge on the artwork was the first treatment considered and was dropped for this reason; the play glyph lives beside the title instead.\n- **Placeholder glyphs are ours, not Apple's**. They appear only when there is no artwork — common for artists — so nothing is ever drawn over a real image.\n- **Artwork bytes are still never copied into our storage**, which the same clause forbids outright. Only the URL is stored.\n\n**The Apple Music Identity Guidelines do not mention album artwork at all.** All 63 sections cover Apple's own badges, lockups, icons, Shazam assets and marketing copy. This is worth writing down because it looks relevant and is not: a search for Apple Music \"badge\" rules returns \"never change the badge artwork in any way\", which is about the _Listen on Apple Music_ button and says nothing about a play glyph on a tile. The two meanings of \"badge\" are easy to conflate and the guidelines are incorporated into the licence by reference, so the mistake looks well-sourced.\n\n### Artwork is cached in memory only — and `AsyncImage` was not\n\nThe clause above forbids _downloading_ MusicKit Content, and the standing rule is that only the artwork URL is stored. **SwiftUI's AsyncImage breaks that rule by default.** It loads through `URLSession.shared`, which uses `URLCache.shared` — and that has a disk capacity as well as a memory one. Every cover a kid scrolled past was being written to disk by the URL loading system, with no code of ours asking for it.\n\nThis one is read from Apple's documented defaults, not measured on a device — it sits above the measured line for that reason. That `URLCache.shared` is disk-backed is not in doubt; the on-disk footprint in this app is unquantified, and a probe that reads the cache directory after a scroll would settle it.\n\nWhat the app does instead: `ArtworkCache` holds decoded images in an `NSCache`, behind a session built from `URLSessionConfiguration.ephemeral` with `urlCache` set to nil — no HTTP cache at all, nothing on the filesystem, and eviction under memory pressure for free. **The same change fixed artwork intermittently never appearing**: `AsyncImage` keeps nothing between appearances, shows its placeholder for a failure as well as a load, and never asks twice, so one lost request among two dozen tiles left a permanent grey square.\n\n### Indirect monetisation — verbatim text for open question 4\n\nThe clause behind research question 4, from the same section. It narrows the question without settling it: the prohibition attaches to monetising _access to the Apple Music service_, not to charging for an application generally.\n\n> You agree not to require payment for or indirectly monetise access to the Apple Music service (e.g. in-app purchase, advertising, requesting user info) through Your use of the MusicKit APIs, MusicKit JS or otherwise in any way.\n\n**Still unanswered, and still blocking business-model decisions.** Whether a paid app that charges for the sandbox rather than for Apple Music falls inside \"otherwise in any way\" is a question for a lawyer, not for reading. What has changed is that the wording is now in hand rather than being recalled second-hand.\n\n## Reading the parent's own library: playlists and artists\n\nEstablished July 2026, while building parent suggestions. Everything below **compiles against the real MusicKit SDK** on macOS — which is a stronger claim than \"recalled from the documentation\" and a weaker one than \"seen working\". The MusicKit capability is still not enabled on the App ID, so none of it has run against a real account.\n\n- `MusicLibraryRequest<Playlist>` and `MusicLibraryRequest<Artist>` both exist and take `.limit`, alongside the `<Song>` and `<Album>` requests already in use. Library seeding was song-and-album only because those are the kinds with codes, not because the other requests were missing.\n- `MusicLibraryRequest<Playlist>` accepts `filter(matching: \\.id, equalTo: MusicItemID(...))`, which is how one playlist is refetched by identifier after crossing out of CatalogKit as a value.\n- A library `Playlist` exposes `name`, `curatorName`, `artwork`, `kind` and `tracks`, and `.with([.tracks])` loads them the same way it does for a catalog playlist. `tracks` is a collection of `Track`, so music videos have to be filtered out — the same `compactMap` that `children(of:)` already does.\n- `Playlist.kind` is `nil` for a playlist the account holder made themselves. Every case of `Playlist.Kind` names something Apple produced, `personalMix` included — that one is a mix Apple built _for_ them, which is not the same thing. **Unverified:** whether a nil kind really is the only marker of an own-made playlist. It decides only a label a parent reads, never what is resolved.\n- **There is still no way to get a catalog identifier for a library item.** No documented property returns one, and for a playlist there is nothing to return — nobody published it. The `PlayParameters`-to-JSON trick that circulates is undocumented, its keys are version-dependent, and it is deliberately not used here.\n\nThat last point forces two things, and both turn out cheaper than the missing identifier suggests. **A playlist is snapshotted track by track** through the ISRC path that already existed, and stored under a local UUID — so the catalog playlist identifier is never needed, not even for one of Apple's. **An artist is derived rather than matched**: `resolveToCatalog` already requests `[.albums, .artists]`, so a resolved song arrives carrying its catalog artist, and naming a library artist means resolving a sample of their songs and reading it off the results. It is right most of the time and wrong in exactly the cases a family library is full of: a track with a guest credit names the guest, a soundtrack names whoever opened it, a ripped compilation names “Various Artists”. So it is a majority vote over roughly ten songs, dropping empty identifiers first, that **refuses rather than guesses** when nothing clears the bar. The asymmetry is worth stating: a suggested artist is an allowed artist, so a wrong answer here hands a child a catalogue nobody chose — where a refusal costs the parent one catalog search.\n\nOne side effect worth noticing: the suggest-a-playlist confirm screen shows the parent “34 of 39 songs matched” before they commit, which makes the ISRC hit rate on a real library something the app reports every time it is used rather than something a hand-run probe has to answer once. Tool reply2026-09-02T15:57:32.347Z
Building the report exposed a live instance of it. The admin's diagnostics screen — unrated frequency, ancestry resolution, how hard the over-fetch loop is working — ran its search through the kid's own `Session.search`, which logs the term and every filtered-out result, and played tracks through the kid's `Session.play`, which logs a refused item as `reach: .reached`. So a parent checking whether a rule worked appeared in the report as their child searching for that term and reaching for that song.

Nobody could have noticed before, because nothing read the log.

It is worse than a wrong number. The report's whole claim is _this is what one child did_, and a parent has no way to tell which rows are theirs. It puts words in a child's mouth, and it does it precisely to the parent who is most engaged — the one who checks their own rules.

**The rule: nothing a parent does writes to the kid's log.** Not searching, not playing, not favoriting, not previewing.

Enforced as a seam rather than a habit, for the same reason the unfiltered read is. Every admin surface goes through a small set of methods that reach the catalog and the player _without_ touching `EventLog`, and any new admin screen belongs there rather than reusing a kid path:

- `searchUnfiltered` — for building a list. No policy applied, nothing logged.
- `previewSearch` — the kid's real policy and the real engine, so a parent sees what their child would get. Nothing logged.
- `previewPlay` — still asks the engine and still refuses what the kid could not play, because the point is showing what the walls do. No block written on refusal, no play written on stop.

The awaited `Session.search` that used to exist has been **deleted rather than left unused.** It had exactly one caller, the one place that must not log, and an unused convenience method that quietly writes to a child's history is a loaded trap for whoever adds the next admin screen.

The one thing preview does not change is the engine. A parent's preview shows the kid's verdict and not a parent's — a preview that could play what the kid cannot would be a screen that lies about the walls it exists to demonstrate.

The production code being gated (quote it, since you're changing it)

/Users/benjaminjordan/projects/thegoldenmule/musicbox/Packages/KidLibrary/Sources/KidLibrary/MergedLibrary.swift:71-88:

// MARK: - Which providers are live

/// `isSharedDevice` alone: false is both providers, true is CloudKit only.
private var liveProviders: [any LibraryProvider] {
    let isShared = device.state.isSharedDevice
    return providers.filter { $0.id == .cloudKit || !isShared }
}

/// Read-live providers, narrower still: a read waits on onboarding's ask.
private var readableProviders: [any LibraryProvider] {
    let hasBeenAsked = device.state.hasBeenAsked
    return liveProviders.filter { $0.id == .cloudKit || hasBeenAsked }
}

/// Providers written for this favorite; a missing capability skips it.
private func writers(favoriting kind: ItemKind) -&gt; [any LibraryProvider] {
    liveProviders.filter { $0.canFavorite(kind) }
}

What it is. Packages/FamilySync is the CloudKit transport layer for household data, added after a design decision recorded in /Users/benjaminjordan/projects/thegoldenmule/musicbox/docs/aural-sandbox/major-pieces/accounts-devices-and-sync.md:177 and /Users/benjaminjordan/projects/thegoldenmule/musicbox/docs/aural-sandbox/major-pieces/storage-and-data-model.md:270: SwiftData mirroring is never used (FamilyStore.container() keeps cloudKitDatabase: .none forever), so SwiftData stays the local authority and CloudKit becomes a transport over it via hand-written CKRecord mapping plus two CKSyncEngine instances. Sources: CloudKitCodec.swift (record mapping), Merge.swift and Reconcile.swift (pure value-in/value-out merge with no CloudKit import), FamilyZone.swift (the zone topology — household zone plus per-kid policy and work zones, because "the topology is the access control": CloudKit has no per-record permissions inside a zone), BindingResolver.swift (pure precedence table deciding which policy is in force), Enrollment.swift, SharePlan.swift, FamilySharing.swift, AccountIdentity.swift, DeviceIdentity.swift, HouseholdSide.swift, SyncEngineHost.swift (whose SyncStateStore / UserDefaultsSyncState are explicitly modeled on DeviceLibraryState — "device-local and never synced, on the same shelf as DeviceLibraryState", SyncEngineHost.swift:6-15).

All of it is in two files. MusicKitLibrarySource lives at the bottom of MusicKitCatalogSource.swift, not its own file.

Packages/CatalogKit/Sources/CatalogKit/LibrarySource.swift

The protocol, in full (:145-166):

/// Seeding shortcut, not a bound on allow; a pick becomes an item or is discarded.
public protocol LibrarySource: Sendable {
    /// Songs and albums only — the only kinds that can match the catalog.
    func libraryItems(kinds: Set&lt;ItemKind&gt;, limit: Int) async throws -&gt; [LibraryItem]

    /// Search within the library.
    func searchLibrary(term: String, kinds: Set&lt;ItemKind&gt;, limit: Int) async throws -&gt; [LibraryItem]

    /// Batched — the one place a parent hands us hundreds of items at once.
    func resolveToCatalog(_ items: [LibraryItem]) async throws -&gt; LibraryImport

    /// The account's own playlists, Apple's and the account holder's alike.
    func libraryPlaylists(limit: Int) async throws -&gt; [LibraryPlaylist]

    /// Tracks, not the playlist — it has no code; resolve yields catalog songs.
    func tracks(of playlist: LibraryPlaylist) async throws -&gt; [LibraryItem]

    /// The account's artists. Names only — an artist carries no code.
    func libraryArtists(limit: Int) async throws -&gt; [LibraryItem]

    /// Names an artist via their songs' ISRCs and ancestry — see ``ArtistVote``.
    func resolveArtist(_ artist: LibraryItem) async throws -&gt; ArtistResolution
}

The last four have empty/.notInAppleMusic defaults (:168-179). Note: LibrarySource is MusicKit-free — it imports only Foundation and PolicyEngine.

Supporting types in the same file: - LibraryItem (:5-37) — id: String (library id, "meaningful only for the length of this flow"), kind: ItemKind, title, subtitle, artworkURL, isrc: String?, upc: String?. No date field. - LibraryPlaylist (:40-67) — id, name, curatorName, trackCount, artworkURL, isPersonal: Bool. - ArtistResolution (:70-78) — .resolved(CatalogItem) / .ambiguous / .notInAppleMusic. - ArtistVote (:81-103) — sample = 10, threshold = 0.5, strict majority over song.ancestors.first { $0.id.kind == .artist }. - DiscardReason (:106-115) — .noIdentifier, .notInAppleMusic, .unsupportedKind. - DiscardedItem (:118-126), LibraryImport (:129-142) — resolved: [CatalogItem], discarded: [DiscardedItem].

ISRC/UPC resolution, the load-bearing part (:508-570): bucket by kind into songsByISRC / albumsByUPC (no code → .noIdentifier; artist/playlist → .unsupportedKind), then exactly two batched requests:

var request = MusicCatalogResourceRequest&lt;Song&gt;(matching: \.isrc, memberOf: codes)
request.properties = [.albums, .artists]
findEquivalentsIfAvailable(&amp;request)

request.properties = [.artists]
findEquivalentsIfAvailable(&amp;request)

Unmatched codes become .notInAppleMusic discards (:562-567).

4. README / doc paragraphs

Packages/CatalogKit/README.md, "Library seeding" (:59-91)

> Lists are built by searching the catalog — FilteredCatalog.search — and any catalog item can go on one, owned or not. The library does not bound what a parent may allow. > > LibrarySource is a shortcut on top of that, for a parent who already owns two hundred suitable records and would rather not type two hundred searches. It saves typing. The kid never browses here, and no library identifier is ever stored. > > resolveToCatalog matches what the parent picked against Apple Music — songs on ISRC, albums on UPC, one batched request each. On iOS and macOS 26.4+ those requests also set .findEquivalents, so a regional pressing or reissue in someone's library still matches the copy their storefront carries. Older systems match more strictly and discard more. […] > > Why the rule matters. If a library identifier could reach an allow or deny list, a deny on an artist would not reach that artist's tracks — no shared namespace to match on, no catalog ancestry to walk. Resolving to the catalog first leaves exactly one namespace, so every rule reaches everything and PolicyEntry needs no scope field. > > Resolved items arrive with ancestry already attached: the match request asks for relationships anyway, so a seeded song is immediately judgeable against a denied artist.

And :105-115: > 2. ISRC and UPC matching assumes library items expose those codes in practice. The properties exist on Song and Album, but how often they are populated for library content — and how often a match actually lands — is exactly what the first real-device run needs to measure. Measure it on a pre-26.4 system too: .findEquivalents is not there to soften the result.

PolicyEngine/README.md — nothing on the library

No occurrence of "librar", "ISRC", "UPC" or "browsing". The nearest relevant rules: :48-52 (artists and playlists skip the rating check — Playlist has no contentRating), :56-59 (a playlist is lineage only when the track is played from it), :64-75 (the unrated problem, UnratedBehavior default .block).

The "never a browsing source" text — CLAUDE.md:364-377

> Three MusicKit affordances are deliberately never used: personalized recommendations, autoplay past the end of a queue, and radio and stations. Each reaches unvetted material. > > A fourth used to be on that list and is now conditional. The user's own library is not a browsing source unless the library is the kid's own, which is what isSharedDevice == false asserts — and that is the default, so the amendment is in force from first launch. Three things carry the original protection across: onboarding asks before the Apple provider's first read, the policy engine judges every item read back, and the read happens only through LibraryProvider, so there is one place the door opens rather than a call site per screen. The library as a seeding input for a parent building lists is untouched — that is still LibrarySource, still ISRC/UPC matching, and no part of it runs through KidLibrary.

Also CLAUDE.md:240-251 (platform floor: MusicLibraryRequest/MusicLibrarySearchRequest force iOS 16; adopt .findEquivalents behind if #available).
